Discussion of the interpretation of His, exalted is He, saying:

[1–4] ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ ﴿which weighed heavily upon your back﴾ ﴿And We raised high your mention﴾

﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ That is: Did We not widen it by casting into it that which gladdens and strengthens him, by making manifest what was hidden from him of wisdoms and rulings, by supporting him and protecting him, until he knew what he had not known, and became the repository of wisdom and the vessel of the realities of the news. The hamza here is for rejecting a negation, and the negation of a negation is an affirmation; for this reason the affirmed statement is conjoined to it.

The root meaning of *sharh* (expansion) is the spreading out of flesh and the like, in which there is a widening that necessarily reveals its inner part and what is hidden within it. *Sharh* and *si'a* (breadth) have been used for the heart, because it is the locus of perception of what gladdens and of its opposite. So its perceiving what contains gladness, which removes what grieves him, is called *sharh* and widening. That is because through inspiration and the like, which relieves his distress and removes his anxiety, what had been absent from him and hidden from him becomes manifest, and in it is his joy, just as one says "*sharaha al-kitab*" (he explained the book) when he clarified it. Then it was applied to the breast, which is the locus of the heart, as an intensification; for the expansion of a thing is followed by the expansion of its container. For this reason you hear people call gladness "*bast*" (spreading out), then they called its opposite "*diq*" (constriction) and "*qabd*" (contraction). This is figurative usage branching from metonymy (*kinaya*) through intermediary steps, and after its currency the concealment disappeared and the intermediaries were removed. This is what al-Shihab verified.

﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ ﴿which weighed heavily upon your back﴾ Al-Shihab said: *al-wizr* is a heavy load. Its *wad'* (putting down) is its removal from him, for when it is construed with *'ala* (upon) it means imposing, and when construed with *min* (from) it means removal. *Al-inqad* is the occurrence of the *naqid*, which is the sound of the vertebrae of the back. It is also said: the sound of the camel, or of the saddle, or of the mount, when it is overloaded. So *al-inqad* is overloading a burden until a *naqid* or a sound is heard from it, as al-Azhari said. Ibn 'Arafa said: it is an overloading which makes what is loaded upon it *naqd*, that is, emaciated and weak. His, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, condition has been exemplified by this, in what weighed upon him and grieved him because of the scarcity of those who responded to his call, the weakness of those who had earlier come to faith in him, the spread of polytheism and misguidance in the Arabian Peninsula, and the strength of its people. And *wad'uhu 'anka* (the removal of it from you) is the multitude of those who afterwards believed, their entry into the religion of Allah in throngs, the strength of his followers, the effacement of polytheism and ignorance from the Peninsula, the humiliation of its people after their might, and their submission after their fierce refusal. It has also been said: the verse is a metonymy for his protection and purification from the filth of sins, like His saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what followed﴾ [al-Fath: 2].

The first view is stronger, and in the verse—in any case—there is an allegorical metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*), and the "putting down" is a supporting complement (*tarshih*) for it.

﴿And We raised high your mention﴾ That is: through prophethood, and the obligation of acknowledging his message, and making it a condition for the acceptance and validity of faith. Qatada said: Allah raised his mention in this world and the Hereafter, so there is no preacher, no one who recites the tashahhud, and no one who performs prayer except that he proclaims: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

And from Mujahid: that is, "I am not mentioned except that you are mentioned with Me." Al-Shihab said: this—that is, what is transmitted from Mujahid—if taken universally, contradicts reality, for Allah has been mentioned alone many times, and the Messenger (ﷺ) has been mentioned alone many times! And if a specific place is designated, it is preference without a preferring factor. And if the matter is taken as unspecified, the defect of vagueness is not hidden.

He said: I have examined it deeply and have not found what cools the breast and turns away the questioner empty-handed, until it appeared to me that the true answer is to say: the mention is to be understood as mention in the assemblies and places of worship; for his mention (ﷺ) is in reality joined with the mention of Allah in them, in the prayers and sermons, so you do not see any gathering of the gatherings of Islam except that it is like this. So his mention (ﷺ) is never separated from the mention of the Exalted in any day of the days, nor any night of the nights, nor even in any time that is counted. Thus the universality is correct. If you say: from where do you have this restriction; is it anything but a preference without a preferring factor? I say: the context speaks with this qualification, for the intended meaning is to honour the mention of him (ﷺ) and to spread his rank, indicating his nearness to his Lord, like the nearness of his name to His name. This is only through mentioning him in gatherings, assemblies, congregational mosques and mosques. And what dissemination is stronger than the adhan (call to prayer)? Not in the markets and roads where every mention is cast.

Then he said: Know that the verification of this matter is what al-Imam al-Shafi'i said at the beginning of his *al-Risala al-Jadida* (the New Epistle), and al-Subki clarified it in his commentary on the Epistle. He said, may Allah have mercy on him:

The Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, said, concerning Mujahid's interpretation of the verse: "I am not mentioned except that you are mentioned with Me": "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Al-Shafi'i said: he means his mention in the faith in Allah and the adhan. It is possible that his mention is also intended in the recitation of the Qur'an, in acting upon obedience, and in abstaining from disobedience.

Al-Subki said: this possibility from al-Shafi'i is very good, and it is based on the meaning of *dhikr* being mention in the heart, which is correct. On this basis it is general, because the one who performs obedience or refrains from disobedience in compliance with the command of Allah, the Exalted, is mentioning the Prophet (ﷺ) in his heart, since he is the one who conveyed them from Allah. This is more general than mention by the tongue, which is restricted to Islam, the adhan, the tashahhud, the sermon and the like. Al-Shafi'i said: No blessing has appeared or remained hidden upon us, by which we have attained a share of religion or worldly life, or by which an adversity in either of them or in one of them has been removed from us, except that Muhammad (ﷺ) is its cause. From this it is known that if the generality and the restriction are kept on their apparent sense, the mention is understood as mention of the heart, and it encompasses every place of worship and obedience. For the believing intelligent person, when he mentions Allah, remembers the one who guided him to knowledge of Him and led him to His obedience, and that is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as has been said:

"You are the gate of Allah; any man who comes to it from other than you, will he enter?"

(p-٦١٩١) You may also say: the intended meaning of raising his mention is to honour him (ﷺ) by mentioning him together with the mention of Allah in the manifest rites of the religion, the first of which are the two words of testimony, which are the foundation of the religion, then the adhan, the prayer, and the sermons. So the restriction is relative. End of al-Shihab's words.

(p-٦١٨٧) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

He said: I have examined it deeply and have not found what cools the breast and turns away the questioner empty-handed, until it appeared to me that the true answer is to say: the mention is to be understood as mention in the assemblies and places of worship; for his mention (ﷺ) is in reality joined with the mention of Allah in them, in the prayers and sermons, so you do not see any gathering of the gatherings of Islam except that it is like this. So his mention (ﷺ) is never separated from the mention of the Exalted in any day of the days, nor any night of the nights, nor even in any time that is counted. Thus the universality is correct. If you say: from where do you have this restriction; is it anything but a preference without a preferring factor? I say: the context speaks with this qualification, for the intended meaning is to honour the mention of him (ﷺ) and to spread his rank, indicating his nearness to his Lord, like the nearness of his name to His name. This is only through mentioning him in gatherings, assemblies, congregational mosques and mosques. And what dissemination is stronger than the adhan (call to prayer)? Not in the markets and roads where every mention is cast.

Then he said: Know that the verification of this matter is what al-Imam al-Shafi'i said at the beginning of his *al-Risala al-Jadida* (the New Epistle), and al-Subki clarified it in his commentary on the Epistle. He said, may Allah have mercy on him:

The Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, said, concerning Mujahid's interpretation of the verse: "I am not mentioned except that you are mentioned with Me": "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Al-Shafi'i said: he means his mention in the faith in Allah and the adhan. It is possible that his mention is also intended in the recitation of the Qur'an, in acting upon obedience, and in abstaining from disobedience.

Al-Subki said: this possibility from al-Shafi'i is very good, and it is based on the meaning of *dhikr* being mention in the heart, which is correct. On this basis it is general, because the one who performs obedience or refrains from disobedience in compliance with the command of Allah, the Exalted, is mentioning the Prophet (ﷺ) in his heart, since he is the one who conveyed them from Allah. This is more general than mention by the tongue, which is restricted to Islam, the adhan, the tashahhud, the sermon and the like. Al-Shafi'i said: No blessing has appeared or remained hidden upon us, by which we have attained a share of religion or worldly life, or by which an adversity in either of them or in one of them has been removed from us, except that Muhammad (ﷺ) is its cause. From this it is known that if the generality and the restriction are kept on their apparent sense, the mention is understood as mention of the heart, and it encompasses every place of worship and obedience. For the believing intelligent person, when he mentions Allah, remembers the one who guided him to knowledge of Him and led him to His obedience, and that is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as has been said:

"You are the gate of Allah; any man who comes to it from other than you, will he enter?"

(p-٦١٩١) You may also say: the intended meaning of raising his mention is to honour him (ﷺ) by mentioning him together with the mention of Allah in the manifest rites of the religion, the first of which are the two words of testimony, which are the foundation of the religion, then the adhan, the prayer, and the sermons. So the restriction is relative. End of al-Shihab's words.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[5–8] ﴿So, indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 6] ﴿So when you are free, strive hard﴾ [al-Sharh: 7] ﴿And to your Lord turn with desire﴾ [al-Sharh: 8]

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿So, indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ point to the fact that what He granted him, may the blessings of God be upon him, of expanding the breast, removing the burden, and raising his remembrance, after the narrowness of the matter and the tightening of the links of distress at the start of the journey, was in accordance with the custom God, may He be exalted, has followed with this kind of creation, namely that with hardship comes ease. For this reason He connected the statement with the particle "fa" (so), which indicates causation. The definite article in "al-'usr" (the hardship) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq, the sense of encompassing all instances), but it encompasses what is known to those addressed, of its individual instances or types. It is the hardship that arises from poverty, weakness, the ignorance of a friend, the strength of an enemy, the scarcity of means to the desired goal, and the like, which are familiar and well known. These types of hardship, however severe they become, while the soul is eager to escape them and seeks to remove their severity, and it employs the means of thought, reflection, and action that are fitting for such situations according to sound reason, and then takes refuge in trust in God so that a first disappointment does not weaken it, and what it meets at the first shock does not break its resolve, then there is no doubt that the soul emerges from them victorious. This was the state of the Prophet ﷺ: the narrowness of the matter upon him led him to thought and reflection, until God gave him what is greater than that, namely revelation and prophethood. Then the opposition of his people did not break any part of his resolve, but he continued to seek wealth in poverty and strength in weakness, until he was given from that what shook the pillars of the Chosroes and the Caesars, and left to his community what they enjoyed for long ages. This was related by the Imam, may God have mercy on him.

A subtle point: the indefiniteness of "yusran" (ease) is for magnification, and the intended meaning is a great ease, which is the ease of both abodes. In the word "ma'a" (with) there is an indication of the extreme swiftness of the coming of ease, as if it were accompanying hardship. So it is a metaphor (isti'arah): resemblance of closeness to accompaniment, so the word "ma'a" is borrowed to mean "after."

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 6] are a repetition for emphasis, or a new promise that hardship is accompanied by another ease, such as the reward of the Hereafter. On this basis it has been transmitted: "Hardship will never overcome two eases." When a definite noun is repeated, the second is the same as the first, whether it is a known referent or a genus. As for an indefinite noun, it is possible that the second refers to a different individual from what was meant by the first.

﴿So when you are free﴾ [al-Sharh: 7], i.e., from one of your beneficial works for yourself and your community, ﴿strive hard﴾ [al-Sharh: 7], i.e., take up another work and exert yourself in it, for you will find the pleasure of rest after toil through the fruit that you gather from the work. This was said by the Imam.

"And to your Lord turn with desire" i.e., in calling to Him, i.e., do not desire anything except His essence, without reward or another aim, so that your call and your guidance are directed to Him. This was said by al-Qashani.

Ibn Jarir said: Make your intention and your desire directed to Him alone, not to anyone else of His creation, since these polytheists of your people had directed their desire in their needs to the gods and rivals. But the more evident view to me, relying on what we have established as correct, that the verse is Medinan (madaniyyah) and among the last of what was revealed, is that the meaning of His words, may He be exalted, (p-6193) ﴿So when you are free, strive hard﴾ [al-Sharh: 7] is: when you have finished fighting the polytheists and achieved your wish from them by the coming of God's help and the victory, then strive hard in worship, glorification, and seeking forgiveness, in gratitude to God for what He has bestowed, and turn to Him alone seeking His pleasure. Thus the two verses have the same meaning as the sura: ﴿When the help of God comes, and the victory﴾ [al-Nasr: 1]. Then I saw that Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from Ibn Zayd, from his father, who said: "So when you are free" means: when you are finished with the jihad, the jihad against the Arabs, and their jihad has ended, then strive hard in the worship of God, and turn to Him. And this is evident. Indeed, the wording of the verse is general, encompassing all that we have related, but the context and parallel passages, which are the most important things to refer to, support what Ibn Zayd said, and we have adopted it. And God knows best.
